analysis.one_liner: Makes the right to vote in federal elections a statutory right and lets voters sue over laws that make voting harder.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with eight cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Rules Committee and never received a hearing, a floor vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare that every citizen of voting age has a fundamental right to vote in federal elections. It would bar federal, state, and local governments from making it meaningfully harder to vote unless the government proves — in court, by clear and convincing evidence — that the restriction serves an important, specific government interest and is the least restrictive way to do it. Voters could challenge restrictive rules in federal court, cases would be expedited, and winning plaintiffs could recover attorney fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who face rules that make registering, casting a ballot, or having it counted more difficult — polling place closures, restrictive ID or registration rules, mail-ballot limits — would get a new tool to challenge those rules quickly in federal court. The protections apply to actions taken by federal, state, and local governments.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that every citizen of legal voting age has a fundamental right to vote in federal elections [S2][S3].

It prohibits governments from substantially impairing the ability to vote in federal elections unless the action significantly furthers an important, particularized government interest, and from diminishing the ability to vote unless it uses the least restrictive means to achieve that interest [S2][S3].
Voters can bring suit in district court, courts must expedite these cases, and a prevailing plaintiff may receive attorney fees [S2][S3].

The law applies to voting rules in effect for elections on or after September 1, 2024, including rules already on the books at enactment, so it could reach restrictions adopted before the bill passed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, and ultimately taxpayers, would bear the cost of defending their election rules in court, paying attorney fees when they lose, and in some cases changing or dropping voting restrictions that courts strike down.
analysis.who_pays_short: State and local governments and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill would put federal courts in the position of reviewing ordinary state election administration decisions, with the government bearing a heavy burden of proof (clear and convincing evidence) once a voter shows a rule makes voting harder — a standard critics of such laws argue goes beyond what courts have applied under the Constitution and raises federalism objections to Congress regulating state election procedures [S2][S3].

The new cause of action, mandatory expedited dockets, and attorney-fee awards could produce a wave of litigation over election rules, with governments — and ultimately taxpayers — paying legal costs even over rules they defend in good faith [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters who have been blocked or burdened by state election restrictions, the bill offers a genuine, enforceable remedy with a fast docket and fee recovery. The trade-offs are real: a heavy burden of proof on governments and attorney fees for winning plaintiffs would make it harder for states to defend many voting rules and would generate substantial litigation. Whether that is a flaw or the point depends on one's view of how much friction in voting is legitimate; the bill's design plainly weighs toward easier access.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ossoff introduced the bill on March 12, 2024, joined by eight cosponsors, all Democrats or independents [S1][S4][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day; that was the only action the bill ever received [S5][S1].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill received no committee vote and no floor vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials who prefer to keep current voting rules free of a federal right-to-vote standard are better off, since the restrictions the bill would have imposed on federal, state, and local election rules never took effect. No organized public group benefited from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials who keep current voting rules

for.name: Sen. Jon Ossoff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sponsor.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past referral in the Senate [S4][S5].
